messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 40
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 49

Carlos, a 40-year-old male of Latin American descent, is a surgeon who lives in the coastal city where he experienced a devastating hurricane two years ago. His marriage remains strong and supportive, but his life has been significantly altered by this traumatic event. On that fateful night, Carlos was on call at the hospital when the winds started to pick up with an intensity he had never witnessed before. The storm surge flooded the streets outside, making it impossible for him to leave. He spent hours working in the emergency room treating patients who were injured during the hurricane. The sounds of howling wind and shattering glass filled his ears as he tried to keep calm and focused. Now, whenever Carlos hears loud, sudden noises or sees heavy rain clouds gathering on the horizon, a wave of anxiety washes over him. He vividly recalls those terrifying moments when the hospital's power went out, leaving them in pitch darkness save for the flickering emergency lights. His hands shake slightly as he recounts how they were forced to rely on backup generators and flashlights while continuing their work. At home, Carlos avoids any mention of weather forecasts or news reports that remind him of the hurricane. He often wakes up in the middle of the night with nightmares, drenched in sweat from reliving the chaos of that night. His wife has noticed how he starts to hyperventilate and freeze whenever there is a loud clap of thunder during summer storms. During his sessions, Carlos describes feeling constantly on edge at work as well. The sterile environment of the operating room usually brings him comfort due to its predictability and control, but lately, even small surprises can trigger an overwhelming sense of dread. He has started avoiding surgery altogether, preferring administrative tasks that allow him to stay away from the OR where the unpredictability feels too similar to those harrowing days. In moments when he is calm enough to reflect, Carlos acknowledges that his performance at work has been affected by these intrusive thoughts and feelings. His focus wavers more easily than before, leading to occasional mistakes during procedures which never used to happen. This self-doubt exacerbates the anxiety; he fears it will only get worse with each passing day. Despite his wife's understanding and support, Carlos finds himself withdrawing from social activities that they once enjoyed together. He no longer wants to go on family beach trips or engage in conversations about their vacation plans for fear of triggering memories associated with the hurricane. His reluctance causes friction between them because he feels guilty about neglecting their relationship but cannot bring himself to face these triggers. Recently, Carlos has started experiencing physical symptoms like headaches and stomachaches more frequently. These pains are often accompanied by intense feelings of guilt over not being able to do enough during that chaotic night at the hospital. He wonders if he could have done something different to prevent some injuries or deaths. His wife notes that recently, he has been more irritable and short-tempered with their children when they get too excited about outdoor activities like camping trips. Carlos knows his reactions are disproportionate but struggles with controlling these outbursts. His frustration stems from an inability to explain the depth of anxiety and fear underlying his responses. Overall, Carlos's life continues to be significantly impacted by the lingering effects of that traumatic hurricane experience. While he remains committed to seeking support through therapy sessions, navigating daily life poses ongoing challenges as he grapples with both external reminders and internal emotional turmoil.
